# The test suite

> The language is tested by `.pcpp` files that describe themselves. `testbed.exe` finds them, builds and runs each one on every target and optimize level, and checks the result. Change the language, add your tests beside the official ones, and run the whole suite to prove you broke nothing.

## Where the tests live

The suite is the folder `bin\res\tests`. Every test is one `.pcpp` file in an area folder:

```
bin\res\tests\
  lex\       the lexical rules: literals, comments, splices
  mod\       modules, imports, initialize / finalize
  dir\       the @ directives
  type\      types, records, objects, sets, choices
  decl\      declarations: const, var, routines, externals
  stmt\      statements
  expr\      expressions and operators
  intr\      the intrinsics
  test\      unit-test blocks and asserts
  cpp\       C++ mixing
  exe\ dll\ lib\   the three build kinds
  std\       the standard library units
  lsp\ dbg\  the language server and the debugger
  suite\     the test system's own tests
```

- A test's id is its folder path under `bin\res\tests`, with `.` between the parts, then its file name without `.pcpp`: `type\type_record.pcpp` is `type.type_record`, and `type\record\type_record_align.pcpp` is `type.record.type_record_align`.
- Sub-folders are for grouping only: put a large area's tests in one sub-folder per concern, `type\record\`, `type\object\`, and the id carries the path.
- A file's name (its stem) is unique in the whole suite, whatever folder it is in: two `type_record.pcpp` files are an error at discovery. Deps name tests by stem.
- Name a test `<area>_<feature>.pcpp`. A test of one mistake is `<area>_<feature>_err_<what>.pcpp`.
- A folder named `fixtures` (any case, any depth) is never searched for tests. A test's inputs go there: units it imports, C and C++ sources, a stdin file, an expected-output file. A `.pcpp` in a fixtures folder is never run as a test.
- A `.pcpp` with no spec block is not a test. It is listed as unspecced and never fails a run.
- Every file carries the project's file header comment, like every other source file.

## The spec block

A test describes itself in one block, anywhere in the file, inside a `/* */` comment:

```
/*
  @@test
    kind run
    expect
    | hello 42
    | [Heap] Allocs: 0, Frees: 0, Leaked: 0
  @@end
*/
```

- `@@test` opens the spec and `@@end` closes it. A file has one spec.
- The spec must sit in a `/* */` comment that is compiled: not in a `//` comment, not in a region a conditional directive switches off, not in a `cppstart` block.
- Keys and values are separated by spaces and line breaks, in any layout.
- `-- text` is a note, to the end of its line.
- A value with spaces or quotes is quoted: `"a b"`. Inside quotes, `\"` is a quote and `\\` a backslash; nothing else is an escape.
- `| text` is one expected line of output. Trailing blanks are trimmed.
- The scanner is strict. An unknown key or value, a key given twice, a missing `@@end`, or a key the kind does not take is a discovery error, reported as `file(line,col)` with a code `TS0001` to `TS0017`. A suite with a discovery error runs nothing.

## Kinds

`kind` is required. It says what the suite does with the file:

| Kind | What the suite does | Passes when |
|---|---|---|
| `run` | builds the program and runs it | it builds, its output equals the `expect` lines, its exit code equals `exitcode` (0 by default) |
| `build` | builds it, never runs it | it builds, with exactly the reports its markers name |
| `error` | compiles it | it reports exactly the mistakes its markers name; with an `ERROR` or `FATAL` marker it must not build |
| `tests` | builds it in unit-test mode and runs it | the program's `Results:` line shows every test passed, and there is at least one test |
| `dep` | builds it only when a test that needs it runs | never a result of its own |
| `unit` | analyzes it, builds nothing | it reports exactly the reports its markers name |
| `cli` | runs `pcpp.exe` itself with `args` | its output equals the `expect` lines and its exit code equals `exitcode` |
| `manual` | nothing: a person checks it by hand in the editor | never a result: `testbed -list -kind manual` lists these files |

- A `manual` file is one only a person can check: what the editor shows (the `lsp_*` files) or what the debugger does (the `dbg_*` files). The suite finds and lists it but never runs it, even when it is named alone.
- A `tests` file turns on `@unitTestMode on;` itself and holds `test` blocks (see [Unit testing](https://paskalcpp.org/docs/testing.html)). A file with no tests fails: a vacuous pass would hide a broken file.
- A `cli` test checks pcpp's own command line. It runs once, on this machine, at `x86_64-windows-gnu`, debug, console.

## Keys

| Key | Value | Kinds |
|---|---|---|
| `kind` | `run` `build` `error` `tests` `dep` `unit` `cli` `manual` | every kind |
| `deps` | the stems of the `dep` tests this test needs | every kind but `cli` |
| `targets` | `x86_64-windows-gnu` and / or `x86_64-linux-gnu` | every kind but `cli` |
| `opt` | `debug` `safe` `fast` `small` | every kind but `cli` |
| `subsystem` | `console` and / or `gui` | every kind but `cli` |
| `define` | `NAME` or `NAME=VALUE`, one or more | every kind but `cli` |
| `warnings` | `allow`: an unmarked hint or warning does not fail the test | every kind but `cli` |
| `args` | one quoted string: the program's arguments (`cli`: pcpp's) | `run` `tests` `cli` |
| `stdin` | a file the program reads as its standard input | `run` `tests` |
| `exitcode` | the program's exit code, 0 or more | `run` `cli` |
| `expect` | `|` lines: the program's whole output | `run` `cli` |
| `expectfile` | a file holding the whole expected output | `run` `cli` |

- With no `targets`, a test runs on both official targets. With no `subsystem`, it is console.
- With no `opt`, a test runs at the optimize level the run asks for with `-opt`, and at `debug` when the run names none. Give `opt` only when the test is about one level, and it runs at those levels only.
- A value list takes each value once: `targets x86_64-windows-gnu x86_64-windows-gnu` is an error.
- `stdin` and `expectfile` paths are relative to the test file's folder: `stdin "fixtures/my_input.txt"`. A missing file is an error at discovery.
- Output that differs by target takes one `expect` per target: `expect x86_64-linux-gnu` and its lines, beside a plain `expect` for every other target. `expectfile` takes a target the same way.

## Expected output

- The program's standard output and standard error are compared together, in the order written.
- Line ends are compared as LF. Trailing blanks on a line, and empty lines at the end, are dropped on both sides. Everything else must match exactly. A failure shows the first line that differs.
- `<DIR>` in an `expect` line stands for the test file's folder, written with `/`. It is how a test expects a path that depends on where the suite is installed. It is not replaced inside an `expectfile`.
- `<OUT>` in an `expect` line stands for the suite's output folder, written with `/` (a `cli` test's pcpp names what it builds there: `| Output: <OUT>/bin/x.exe`). It is not replaced inside an `expectfile`.
- A `cli` test's expected output is all of pcpp's output, its build lines included. Colours, a window title a program leaves, and pcpp's `Building <name>... <N>s` progress lines (their number depends on the machine) are taken out before the comparison.
- A program runs in its own output folder, with the spec's `args`. With no `stdin` its standard input is empty.
- In a debug build the runtime prints its heap report when the program ends, `[Heap] Allocs: N, Frees: N, Leaked: N`, so write it where it appears, usually the last expected line (a DLL's report comes when the DLL unloads, before the host's later lines). Other optimize levels do not print it, and the suite leaves every `[Heap]` line out of the expected output when it runs the test at those levels: one expectation serves every level.

## Report markers

A test that expects a diagnostic says so on the line the diagnostic points at, with a marker in a comment:

```
  GCount: int32; // ERROR SM0004@3: is already declared in this scope
```

- The form is `SEVERITY CODE@COLUMN: text`. The severity is `HINT`, `WARN`, `ERROR` or `FATAL`. The code is the diagnostic's code. `@COLUMN` and `: text` are optional; when given, the column must match, and the text must be the start of the message.
- A marker stands on the line of its comment, and one comment may hold several markers.
- A test's reports must match its markers exactly: every report needs a marker, and every marker needs its report. clang's reports count the same as the compiler's.
- An unmarked hint or warning fails the test, unless the spec says `warnings allow`.
- An `ERROR` or `FATAL` marker is allowed in an `error` test only. An `error` test needs at least one marker. Every other kind must build.
- A line no `//` comment can end (one that ends in a line splice, or a `#` line) takes its marker in a block comment whose text begins with `//`: `/* // WARN LX0201@44 */`. A block comment that does not begin with `//` is never read as a marker, so a description can show a marker without being one.
- One mistake per `error` test: a file with many mistakes tests the compiler's recovery, and only recovery tests do that on purpose.

## Dependencies

A test that links a library or a DLL the suite must build first names it in `deps`:

```
  @@test
    kind run
    deps my_scale_lib
    expect
    | 6 x 7 = 42
  @@end
```

- The library is its own file, `my_scale_lib.pcpp`, a `lib` or `dll` module whose spec says `kind dep`.
- Before each run of the consumer, the suite builds its deps in that run's own target and optimize level, in dependency order, so the library is always the one built for the cell being tested.
- Every build writes into `bin\output`: programs in `output\bin`, libraries in `output\lib`. A consumer finds its dep with `@addlibrarypath "$P:output/lib";` and `@linklibrary "my_scale_lib";`.
- Selecting a test selects its deps with it.
- Discovery checks the graph: a dep that does not exist, a cycle (the whole chain is shown), a dep that cannot build the consumer's target or level, and a `dep` test no test names are errors.

## The live examples

`bin\res\tests\suite` holds one working test of each kind. They run with every suite run, so they are always current. Copy the one closest to your test:

| File | Shows |
|---|---|
| `suite_run.pcpp` | a `run` test |
| `suite_build.pcpp` | a `build` test |
| `suite_error.pcpp` | an `error` test and its marker |
| `suite_tests.pcpp` | a `tests` program |
| `suite_dep.pcpp` + `suite_dep_lib.pcpp` | a test with a dep, and the dep |
| `suite_unit.pcpp` | a `unit` test |
| `suite_stdin.pcpp` | `stdin` from `fixtures\` |
| `suite_cli_missing.pcpp` | a `cli` test with `<DIR>` |
| `suite_dir.pcpp` | `<DIR>` in a run test |

## Running the suite

Run `testbed.exe` from the `bin` folder:

```
testbed -all                                   every test, every cell (each target at every optimize level)
testbed type.type_record                       one test
testbed "type.*"                               every test of an area
testbed "type.type_record*"                    a glob over ids
testbed -from expr.expr_a -to expr.expr_m      a range, in id order
testbed -all -t x86_64-windows-gnu             one target
testbed -all -opt fast                         one optimize level (repeat -opt for more)
testbed -all -kind error                       one kind
testbed -failed                                only what failed in the last run
testbed -list "lex.*"                          list the tests (-v: every cell)
testbed -root C:\my\tests -all                 only the tests under one folder
testbed -rpc status                            the running testbed's progress, as JSON
testbed -rpc stop                              stop the running testbed cleanly
testbed -rpc wait 600                          wait for it to finish (its exit code)
testbed -h                                     every option
```

- The exit code is 0 when everything passed, 1 when something failed, 2 for bad arguments, and 3 when the run was stopped. `-rpc` adds 4 when no testbed is running and 5 when `-rpc wait` runs out of time.
- A run goes cell by cell: every test on Windows at debug, then at safe, fast and small, then the same on Linux, so each target's toolchain and build cache stay warm instead of every test switching targets.
- One testbed runs per output folder: a second one started while the first runs is refused with TS0111.
- A running testbed answers `testbed -rpc <command>` from another console: `status` (the cell, the test, the counts and how long since it last checked in, as one JSON line), `failures` (the failed tests so far, as JSON), `stop` (the same as the stop key: the running test finishes, nothing more starts), `abort` (the same as pressing it twice) and `wait [seconds]` (until the run ends; exits with the run's own exit code).
- To stop a run cleanly, press `Ctrl+Shift+Alt+X` (it works from any window, so it also stops a run with no console) or create the file `bin\output\testbed.stop`. The test that is running finishes, nothing more starts, and the summary says `STOPPED after N of M`. Press again (or create the file again) to end the running test at once: its processes are ended and it is listed as skipped, `stopped`. `Ctrl+C` is not a clean stop.
- A run prints one line per test and cell, and the first difference of each failure, then the totals. The last run's results are kept in `bin\output\testsuite-results.txt`, which `-failed` reads.
- Linux tests run through WSL. On a machine without WSL they are skipped with the reason, never counted as passed.
- Builds share one output folder, so tests build one at a time.
- A glob selects ids, so it starts with the area: `"mod.mod_kinds*"`. A bare `"mod_kinds*"` matches nothing.
- `-list` takes the same filters as a run and shows the cells that run would use: `testbed -list -v -opt fast "lex.*"` lists each lex test at fast. A test the filters leave with no cell is not listed.

## Validating a language change

1. Write the feature's test: one `run` test that uses the feature and prints what proves it worked, and one `error` test per mistake the compiler must report for it.
2. Run them alone until they pass: `testbed mod.mod_my_feature mod.mod_my_feature_err_twice`.
3. Run your area on both targets: `testbed "mod.*"`.
4. Run the whole suite, one target and optimize level at a time. The toolchain caches its work per target and level, so this order reuses the cache for every test of a pass:

```
testbed -all -t x86_64-windows-gnu -opt debug
testbed -all -t x86_64-windows-gnu -opt fast
testbed -all -t x86_64-windows-gnu -opt small
testbed -all -t x86_64-windows-gnu -opt safe
testbed -all -t x86_64-linux-gnu -opt debug
testbed -all -t x86_64-linux-gnu -opt fast
testbed -all -t x86_64-linux-gnu -opt small
testbed -all -t x86_64-linux-gnu -opt safe
```

5. Fix what fails, then rerun just that with `testbed -failed`.

- A failing test is a defect to fix, in the compiler or in the test, never a check to weaken.
- A change that is not seen in pcpp's output, exit code or diagnostics is not tested yet: make the test print it.
